title: A Synapse That Does Not Wait

scenes.tts: Many irregular fibres start at type one hair cells, each wrapped in a cup-shaped ending called a calyx. Could this synapse help make them fast?
scenes.caption: Many irregular fibres start at type I hair cells, each wrapped in a cup-shaped ending called a calyx. Could this synapse help make them fast?
scenes.visual: Title card: A Synapse That Does Not Wait. A flask-shaped hair cell inside a cup-shaped calyx. Question: could this synapse help make them fast?
scenes.narration: Many irregular fibres start at type I hair cells, each wrapped in a cup-shaped ending called a calyx. Could this synapse help make them fast?

scenes.tts: A type one cell is flask-shaped, almost enclosed by its calyx. A type two cell is cylindrical, with small boutons.
scenes.caption: A type I cell is flask-shaped, almost enclosed by its calyx. A type II cell is cylindrical, with small boutons.
scenes.visual: The lesson figure: type I cell in its calyx beside a type II cell touching several boutons.
scenes.narration: A type I cell is flask-shaped, almost enclosed by its calyx. A type II cell is cylindrical, with small boutons.

scenes.tts: Calyx-only fibres, and many irregular fibres, come from each organ's central zone. Type one cells occur in both zones. That is a population pattern.
scenes.caption: Calyx-only fibres, and many irregular fibres, come from each organ's central zone. Type I cells occur in both zones. That is a population pattern.
scenes.visual: An organ-specific schematic of a crista: central zone shaded, with calyx-only endings; irregular fibres leave it; type I cells drawn in both zones. Label: population pattern, not a rule.
scenes.narration: Calyx-only fibres, and many irregular fibres, come from each organ's central zone. Type I cells occur in both zones. That is a population pattern.

scenes.tts: A tempting shortcut says type one cells release no vesicles. Wrong. Both types release glutamate from vesicles.
scenes.caption: A tempting shortcut says type I cells release no vesicles. Wrong. Both types release glutamate from vesicles.
scenes.visual: A struck-through card: type I non-vesicular. Then both cells show ribbons with vesicles.
scenes.narration: A tempting shortcut says type I cells release no vesicles. Wrong. Both types release glutamate from vesicles.

scenes.tts: In sustained release, type one cells in mature mouse tissue released about ten times less than type two cells.
scenes.caption: In sustained release, type I cells in mature mouse tissue released about ten times less than type II cells.
scenes.visual: Two release bars; the type I bar is about a tenth of the type II bar. Label: mature mouse utricle, capacitance.
scenes.narration: In sustained release, type I cells in mature mouse tissue released about ten times less than type II cells.

scenes.tts: Now a second route. Non-quantal transmission is a change in calyx voltage with no vesicle fusion and no gap junctions.
scenes.visual: Definition card: non-quantal transmission, no vesicle fusion, no gap junctions.
scenes.narration: Now a second route. Non-quantal transmission is a change in calyx voltage with no vesicle fusion and no gap junctions.

scenes.tts: At a chemical synapse, a vesicle must fuse, glutamate must cross, and receptors must open. Each step adds delay.
scenes.visual: Three steps animate in turn with a small clock ticking at each: fuse, diffuse, open.
scenes.narration: At a chemical synapse, a vesicle must fuse, glutamate must cross, and receptors must open. Each step adds delay.

scenes.tts: Pause and predict. Remove otoferlin, or a calcium channel that release needs. Can a type one cell still make its calyx fire?
scenes.caption: Pause and predict. Remove otoferlin, or a calcium channel that release needs. Can a type I cell still make its calyx fire?
scenes.visual: Knockout card: no otoferlin, or no CaV1.3. Question: can the calyx still fire?
scenes.narration: Pause and predict. Remove otoferlin, or a calcium channel that release needs. Can a type I cell still make its calyx fire?

scenes.visual: the question stays on screen

scenes.tts: Yes. Without either protein, type one cells still made the calyx fire, in mouse tissue in a dish.
scenes.visual: The calyx trace still shows spikes. Label: Spaiardi and colleagues, 2022; in vitro.
scenes.narration: Yes. Without either protein, type I cells still made the calyx fire, in mouse tissue in a dish.
scenes.caption: Yes. Without either protein, type I cells still made the calyx fire, in mouse tissue in a dish.

scenes.tts: The test was whether spikes survive, not whether the signal is normal.
scenes.visual: Caption: spikes survive; normal signal not tested.
scenes.narration: The test was whether spikes survive, not whether the signal is normal.

scenes.tts: How could that work? The cleft between the cell and its calyx is very narrow.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the thin cleft between hair-cell membrane and calyx inner membrane.
scenes.narration: How could that work? The cleft between the cell and its calyx is very narrow.

scenes.tts: When the hair cell depolarizes, more potassium current flows out into that thin space. Potassium slowly builds up there.
scenes.visual: Potassium dots stream into the cleft and accumulate gradually; a potassium-concentration gauge rises slowly.
scenes.narration: When the hair cell depolarizes, more potassium current flows out into that thin space. Potassium slowly builds up there.

scenes.tts: Raise potassium in the cleft, and potassium's reversal potential at the calyx moves up.
scenes.visual: On screen, illustrative: 140 mM inside; cleft 7 mM gives about minus 80 mV; cleft 20 mM gives about minus 52 mV.
scenes.narration: Raise potassium in the cleft, and potassium's reversal potential at the calyx moves up.

scenes.tts: With the other conductances held fixed, this shift tends to depolarize the calyx.
scenes.visual: A balance-point pointer slides upward as the potassium reversal potential rises. Label: steady-state, fixed-conductance illustration. Separate gauges for cleft potassium concentration and cleft electrical potential; inner-face driving force shown as V calyx minus V cleft minus E_K.
scenes.narration: With the other conductances held fixed, this shift tends to depolarize the calyx.

scenes.tts: The current also makes the cleft itself positive, quickly. Less potassium leaves the calyx, or some enters, so it depolarizes.
scenes.visual: A separate cleft-potential gauge jumps quickly, ahead of the slow potassium gauge; the outward potassium arrow at the calyx shrinks, then flips inward.
scenes.narration: The current also makes the cleft itself positive, quickly. Less potassium leaves the calyx, or some enters, so it depolarizes.

scenes.tts: We met potassium first, but in a model, the cleft potential acts first and potassium later. That order is a prediction.
scenes.visual: Timeline: cleft potential, then potassium. Label: model output, Govindaraju and colleagues; not a measurement.
scenes.narration: We met potassium first, but in a model, the cleft potential acts first and potassium later. That order is a prediction.

scenes.tts: Keep the evidence apart. Mouse knockouts and young rat calyces are measurements.
scenes.visual: Evidence table rows build: mouse, measured; neonatal rat, measured.
scenes.narration: Keep the evidence apart. Mouse knockouts and young rat calyces are measurements.

scenes.tts: So are turtle recordings of both cells together, which found a slow coupling and a much faster one.
scenes.visual: Third row: turtle dual patch, slow and fast coupling, both directions. Fourth row: model, predicted.
scenes.narration: So are turtle recordings of both cells together, which found a slow coupling and a much faster one.

scenes.tts: Two routes leave a type one cell. One waits for vesicles. One does not.
scenes.caption: Two routes leave a type I cell. One waits for vesicles. One does not.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: two routes, one that waits for vesicles and one that does not.
scenes.narration: Two routes leave a type I cell. One waits for vesicles. One does not.
